item.title: ‘The bottleneck used to be dumpling-folding talent’: Din Tai Fung CEO on America’s top-grossing restaurant chain turning craft into corporate training
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: demonstrates original reporting and clear structure

The restaurant chain with the highest per-store sales in America says the thing that used to limit its growth was a labor shortage of a very specific kind. Anyone who’s had the soup dumplings at the memorable chain can attest to seeing the lab-coated technicians behind the glass windows working their magic.

“The bottleneck used to be dumpling-folding talent,” Albert Yang, CEO of Din Tai Fung North America, told Fortune by email. “But through continuous improvements to our training programs, we’ve largely overcome that challenge.”

Dumpling-folding talent is a phrase with a lot of history behind it. For most of the time Chinese food has been sold in America, the people folding it were family: the owner, the spouse, the kids and, as Lucas Sin, chef at the New York chain Junzi Kitchen, put it in a 2020 Fortune roundtable, “a cousin of a cousin of a cousin from Fujian.”

At Din Tai Fung, folding is now a corporate job track: a 12-week training program, and a dumpling training manager in every U.S. restaurant, Yang told the Los Angeles Times in 2023.

That swap, from family labor to systems, is reshaping Chinese food in America. Din Tai Fung’s U.S. restaurants averaged $27.4 million in sales in 2024, nearly double the next-closest chain, according to Technomic data reported by Restaurant Business. Panda Express, co-run by an engineer who built her own point-of-sale system in the 1980s, now tops $6 billion a year.

Free labor was the business model

The old Chinese-American restaurant, as the people who ran it describe it, depended on cheap labor at the start and a ready buyer at the end.

“You could always hand it off to the next wave of immigrants. Toisan to Hong Kong to Taiwan to Fujian,” Jennifer 8. Lee, author of The Fortune Cookie Chronicles, said in a 2020 Fortune roundtable on the state of New York’s Chinese restaurants. “But now it’s pretty good in China. Why go into debt coming to America and buying a restaurant?”

Foreign Policy reported in 2019 the waves of migrants from rural Fujian, who had staffed takeout kitchens in the 1980s and 1990s had died down as living conditions in China improved. Wages for takeout cooks had climbed from about $1,500 a month in the 1980s to close to $4,000. The family side ran out too. A 2019 New York Times analysis of Yelp data found Chinese restaurants fell from 7.3% to 6.5% of all restaurants across the 20 largest U.S. metro areas over five years, about 1,200 fewer places, as owners retired and their college-educated kids took other jobs.

“There was no succession plan, because success was seen as not having to do it anymore,” Jason Wang, cofounder of Xi’an Famous Foods, said in the Fortune roundtable.

The pressure hasn’t eased. In 2025, chain restaurant sales grew at their slowest pace outside the pandemic since the Great Recession, and Restaurant Business listed an immigration crackdown among the reasons, along with weak consumer confidence, weight-loss drugs and bad weather, in its Technomic Top 500 coverage.

Yang tells the demand side through his own childhood. Many Americans, he said, first met Chinese food at cheap fast-food and fast-casual spots opened by immigrants who couldn’t afford beautiful dining rooms.

“They were focused on surviving, supporting their families, and building a future for the next generation,” he said.

But now, the Chinese food offered by his family’s company is downright aspirational.

“I remember growing up, my mom would pack me Chinese food for lunch, and other kids would sometimes make fun of me for it,” he said. “Now, I hear from parents that their kids actually think it’s cool when someone brings leftover Din Tai Fung to school for lunch.”

Din Tai Fung was inducted into the Asian Hall of Fame this month as a “Global Family Legacy” honoree; Albert and Aaron Yang accepted on behalf of the family at the Nov. 5 ceremony in Los Angeles.

Systems win

The Chinese food businesses that have scaled in America are the ones that replaced family labor with process early.

Panda Express is a top example. Andrew Cherng’s family opened Panda Inn in Pasadena in 1973, and business was so slow at first his mother would sprinkle salt on the threshold to chase off evil spirits, he said at Nation’s Restaurant News’ CREATE conference in July. His wife, Peggy Cherng, is an engineer by training. When point-of-sale systems barely existed in the mid-1980s, she built one.

“We had to develop it ourselves,” she said. Panda now has more than 2,600 U.S. locations, more than $6 billion in annual sales, and its own Panda University for employees—ranking it 11th among U.S. chains.

People in the business saw this coming years ago.

“Automation and central kitchens will take over,” Wong of the culinary federation told Foreign Policy in 2019. Zhao predicted takeouts would be consolidated under new brands that keep prices low through automation.

The newest arrivals come with systems already built. Chinese chains including HeyTea, Chagee, Luckin Coffee, Wallace, and Haidilao, some with thousands of stores at home, have pushed into U.S. cities to escape a price war in a saturated home market, the Times reported in December 2025.

“China’s food service industry is suffering from severe oversupply,” Bob Qing, founder of the restaurant investor Tomato Capital, told the paper. Limited-service Asian and noodle chains grew U.S. sales 7.8% in 2025, faster than any other segment, according to Technomic data reported by Restaurant Business.

Turning a craft into a job description

Din Tai Fung is the cleanest example, because its whole product is the thing that’s hardest to systematize. Each Din Tai Fung restaurant turns out about 10,000 dumplings a day with roughly 30 chefs on rotation, each dumpling held to 18 folds and 21 grams, the LA Times reported in 2023. Kan Kuang-Ming, the chain’s head chef in Taiwan, told the paper: “You have to fail about 1,400 times before you can make one that is beautiful.”…

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-21 13:30 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Workers pay all of the $28,303 family health plan. Their benefits consultants earn more when it rises
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: highly relevant to business and health, with clear reporting

The average employer-sponsored family health plan now costs $28,303. Workers see about a quarter of this cost in their paycheck and assume that their employer pays the rest. The rude shock is that workers pay all of it.

When an employer thinks about hiring someone, they think in terms of total compensation, not the individual buckets such as cash wages, paid leave, retirement benefits, workers’ compensation premiums, and health insurance. When the cost of one of these items balloons, the others grow less. Economists have documented the trade-off between wages and fringe benefits for decades. Thus, inevitably, rising health insurance premiums crowd out cash wage growth.

Nowadays, the cost of an average family health plan is 44 percent of the typical full-time worker’s (pre-tax) cash wages. You would think somebody would push back on these costs on behalf of workers. Sadly, almost no one is. The real question is why, and what can be done about it.

It’s important to clarify that roughly 100 million people get their health benefits from large companies that self-insure their health plan. That is, the employer doesn’t buy health insurance; rather, it pays the health care bills for its workers and family members. So this is not a story about insurers gouging employers on premiums. Insurers are just hired administrators.

Instead, let’s start with the people large employers are paying to design their benefits. Most large self-insured companies use a handful of big benefits consultants to coordinate and manage health benefit design and contracting. There’s a very good chance these consultants look out for their own interests first and foremost, rather than the companies’, let alone the workers’ interests.

Begin with how “value” is measured. For hospitals, the standard approach is to examine the discounts hospitals provide off their billed charges. This almost makes sense, but hospital charges are widely known to be nonsense values set by the hospitals themselves and charged to virtually no one. Highmark, a Blue Cross plan, makes this exact point in its own employer materials: a facility that charges $100 and gives a 60% discount is paid $40, while one that charges $70 and gives a 50% discount is paid $35. The bigger discount costs more. Milliman, an actuarial firm, notes that charges are far less constrained than negotiated prices and thus rise faster, so discounts appear to grow larger at the same time prices rise.

The same pattern is evident throughout the health plan. Out-of-network claims are often repriced by vendors paid a percentage of the “savings” off billed charges, as a 2024 investigation of MultiPlan documented. The higher the bill, the bigger the fee. Drug benefits have long been judged by rebates off list prices set by manufacturers.

In every case, the rewards go to whoever sets the highest list price. The price that matters is the price actually paid for health care, net of any discounts. This is the equivalent of withholding more in taxes throughout the year only to be delighted with your large tax refund next year. Employers need to judge prices against a benchmark the provider doesn’t control, such as Medicare prices.

Additionally, large companies need to interrogate their benefits consultants on how exactly they are being paid. Federal law requires that brokers and consultants disclose their direct and indirect compensation, but not necessarily how the incentives are structured. If benefits consultant revenue rises with employer spending, or is higher for the vendors it recommends, employers have their answer.

What about the corporate benefits department? Isn’t it their job to directly interface with the consultants and monitor this? They need shaking up, because their incentives are all wrong. Corporate benefits staff are in a difficult position. If health plan changes go wrong, they get all the complaints, often with the CEO copied. If their decisions save the company (and its workers) millions of dollars, they get none of that. From their perspective, there is only downside risk. So they avoid any change that might generate complaints. Nobody gets fired for sticking with the status quo.

Meanwhile, workers are paying the bill. But their costs are diffuse and nearly invisible. Their share of the health plan cost is commonly spread across 26 paychecks. That’s a few hundred dollars per biweekly pay period. This is minimally salient to them. This is the classic case of concentrated blame and diffuse, hidden costs. Absent some outside pressure to change, the benefits office is doing exactly what its incentives reward.

None of this requires new legislation. It does require a sustained, CFO-level effort, because anyone else will bear the brunt of any pushback and get none of the reward. The following represents the minimum necessary steps to take charge of the situation:

- Finance needs to be at the table. Treat the health plan like any other line item of this size, with the same scrutiny of contracts, prices and vendor margins.

- Change the benchmark. Negotiated prices are more available than ever thanks to health care price transparency. Use that information to insist on meaningful comparisons against an external benchmark, such as a multiple of Medicare. Note that Medicare prices are only a benchmark, not an aspirational price.

- Pay your consultant a flat, disclosed fee. No more commissions tied to premiums, and no more side payments from vendors they recommend.

- Make employees your partners. Workers have every reason to be suspicious. If this looks like another cost grab, it will fail. Commit up front that savings will show up as lower contributions and higher take-home pay, and report the numbers to employees every year.…

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-21 13:30 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Billionaires are tearing down L.A. mansions to build bigger ones—and pricing out mere millionaires
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting topic, but lacks depth and detail

California’s rich are rebuilding Los Angeles into a mecca of palatial opulence, and the very richest are pushing everyone else out of the way, including ordinary millionaires.

While the broader housing market is losing buyers as mortgage rates climb toward 7%, L.A.’s wealthiest residents are still throwing down for their dream estates. Not even the prospect of a billionaire tax slowed them. A handful of billionaires left the state ahead of the vote, but California voters rejected Proposition 40, a proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth, on Nov. 3.

With open lots hard to come by, the ultra-wealthy have found their own solution: buy an existing (and already expensive) home, tear it down, and build a far bigger one in its place. The result is a widening split at the top of the market, where billionaires are outbidding the merely rich for a shrinking supply of trophy land.

“They’re shopping for privacy and acreage – and then also things like ocean views, security, and the ability to build exactly what they want,” says Daniel Amodeo, president of Amo Realty in Los Angeles. “A multimillion-dollar house might be purchased just to tear it down and build something substantially larger. When money isn’t an object, the value of the existing house can become secondary to the land underneath it.”

The money is concentrated in a handful of ZIP codes

California claims six of the 10 most expensive ZIP codes in the country, according to a Realtor.com ranking of January 2026 listings. Newport Coast tops the list with a median list price of $12.5 million, followed by Beverly Hills at No. 3 with $10.5 million. Bel-Air comes in at $7.9 million, and Montecito, where Oprah Winfrey and Prince Harry live, at $6.5 million. Rancho Santa Fe and Newport Beach round out the state’s share of the top 10.

The same pressure shows up across the state’s biggest metros. In a 2025 analysis, Zillow ranked San Jose, Los Angeles and San Francisco as the three most expensive U.S. metros for luxury homes.

“We’re seeing a growing divide at the very top of California’s luxury real estate market,” says Mauricio Umansky, CEO and founder of The Agency. “Billionaire buyers are willing to pay a premium for privacy, prime locations and larger estates, particularly in areas like Beverly Hills, Bel Air and Malibu. That’s driving up prices and creating more competition for a limited number of properties.”

It’s not all old wealth, either. Much of it is new tech money. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and his wife, Wendy, paid $110 million for the Spelling Manor in Holmby Hills in 2025. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong is the proud owner of a $133 million Bel-Air estate he bought in late 2021. And Amazon’s Jeff Bezos snapped up the historic Warner Estate in Beverly Hills for $165 million in 2020.

“The world’s wealthiest buyers are increasingly looking beyond traditional measures of size and finishes and placing a premium on scarcity, exclusivity and the ability to create a truly individual living experience,” says Kristina Quesada, co-founder of the Yost Quesada Team at Douglas Elliman in Del Mar.

For some billionaires, one home isn’t enough. WhatsApp cofounder Brian Acton spent $86.3 million on seven houses in Palo Alto, while cofounder Jan Koum spent $57 million across five deals to assemble a compound in Atherton. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg spent more than $110 million on at least 11 houses in Palo Alto’s Crescent Park neighborhood.

Wildfires turned burned lots into a land market

The January 2025 fires, which helped make last year the costliest wildfire year on record, opened up a new supply of land. Investors bought roughly 40% of the vacant lots that sold in Pacific Palisades, Altadena and Malibu in the third quarter of 2025, according to Redfin.

New Zealand billionaires Mat and Nick Mowbray, founders of toymaker Zuru, bought 16 burned beachfront lots in Malibu and plan to fill them with prefab homes made in their company’s factory, a plan that has unsettled longtime residents. Powerball winner Edwin Castro took a different approach, spending about $10 million on 15 Eaton Fire lots in his hometown of Altadena to rebuild homes and sell them to families who want to live there.

The Los Angeles Times calls the broader trend gentrification by billionaire, but it goes by other names, too, depending on whom you ask. Developers call it spec redevelopment. Opponents call it mansionization.

“At the highest end, buyers aren’t simply looking for a bigger house,” says Quesada. “They’re looking for something they cannot easily replicate elsewhere, whether that’s an extraordinary parcel of land, a protected ocean view or the ability to create a completely customized residence.”

Neighbors and regulators are pushing back

Not everyone is thrilled with this wave of hyper-development. Neighbors complain about encroaching mansions that block their views, environmentalists warn of ecological damage, and preservationists fight the sale and demolition of historic properties.

Sometimes the fight goes to court. Milwaukee Brewers owner Mark Attanasio was accused in 2024 of taking sand from Malibu’s public Broad Beach to shore up his roughly $30 million beachfront property. This fall, his company agreed with the California Coastal Commission to restore the shoreline and dedicate a $2 million beachfront lot to the public.

Homeowner groups are using zoning, too. In Beverly Grove, residents spent the better part of a decade fighting teardowns before winning a 2013 city ordinance that caps home size in the neighborhood. Other neighborhood associations have pursued historic preservation overlay zones to slow demolitions.

“Even buyers with $10 million or $20 million to spend are finding that their money doesn’t go as far as it once did in these markets,” says Umansky.

A state of extremes…

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-21 13:18 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Sessions offer advice on rising energy costs

- Published

A charity is offering free advice on energy bills with prices expected to climb further from January.

Devon Communities Together said it was hosting drop-in sessions across the county, which include help with energy bills, smart meters and switching suppliers.

Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to rise by Â£443 a year from January. Heating oil prices have also risen drastically since the start of this year, from about 60p to Â£1.11 a litre, according to the Action with Communities in Rural England network.

Devon County Council said many households in rural parts relied on heating oil because they were not connected to mains gas.

Nora Corkery, chief executive of Devon Communities Together, said: "Behind every statistic is a household making difficult choices: rationing the heating, putting off filling up a tank, or cutting back on journeys they can't really do without."

The charity said people could access confidential one-to-one support to find financial help, with a limited number of free winter warm packs available for those who attend.

Cheryl Cottle-Hunkin, from Devon County Council, said: "I'd urge anyone who is struggling, or worried about the winter ahead, to seek advice and find out what help may be available."

Amando Komoda runs a Minneapolis company that sells supplies for dry-aging meat, and he uses an AI agent called Instinct to set up alerts for hard-to-find parts, such as a particular Raspberry Pi chip, so he doesn't have to search for them himself. item.title: Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: important topic, but lacks depth and detail

Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad

"This building is hell on Earth," says Phil, describing the black mould and rats at Castleview House, the block of flats in Runcorn, Cheshire, where he lives.

But to an estate agent called BritskÃ© Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity.

The estate agent's marketing material said the flat was a government-funded source of income for investors, where tenants were taken care of and the property was in excellent condition.

A Czech investor bought it last year for Â£163,150, more than double the Â£75,000 cost of similar apartments in the block.

The BBC has found more than 40 companies marketing similar properties to individuals in the UK and abroad, as businesses seek to profit from a government system intended to provide housing and support for vulnerable people.

About a dozen of these companies work with a property developer called Lee Jones, whose company sold Phil's flat.

The homes they are selling to investors are advertised as supported accommodation, a type of housing for people with issues including mental health problems or drug abuse issues, as well as people fleeing domestic violence.

Providers offering what is known as supported exempt accommodation are allowed to charge the taxpayer more than the usual housing benefit cap, because they have higher running costs. Tenants are entitled to care, support and supervision - although how much support should be provided is not defined.

While there are legitimate providers helping people back into independent living, the BBC has previously reported on how some are exploiting the system by taking the higher housing benefit payments but failing to provide support.

Our latest investigation found companies marketing supported housing properties to people in Hong Kong, Macau, Nigeria, Turkey, the Netherlands, the UK and other countries as a "secure", "government-backed" investment.

We also found adverts made misleading promises about the quality of the accommodation and support, with tenants saying they were receiving little or no care, while we observed examples of poor quality, unsafe accommodation.

Housing charities and experts have told the BBC the sector has been transformed into a profit-generating machine at the expense of some tenants' safety, care, and dignity.

Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Housing Select Committee, said it was "outrageous" that supported housing properties were being marketed as investments "particularly where there's public funds involved".

The BBC's findings were "alarming" and showed a sector "open to abuse", she added.

'Total dishonesty' in marketing

Lee Jones's company The Investment Room converted Castleview House in 2019 from an office block into more than 200 residential flats, including the one where Phil now lives.

Then Jones partnered with Nurture Housing Association. His company granted Nurture a 25-year-lease on some of the flats, to provide housing for people on government benefits. Jones has a close business relationship with Nurture's chief executive Chris Smith, with the pair also acting as joint directors of other housing companies.

Jones then worked with estate agents, which marketed the housing to investors in the UK and overseas using the regular cashflow generated by the 25-year lease with Nurture and the promise of government funding to justify inflated prices.

Lee Jones and Nurture have repeated this with property developments across England, including in Doncaster, Rotherham, Stockton-on-Tees and Bradford. These type of properties are also in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland but are funded and regulated differently.

Because neither profit-making private companies nor individuals can act as supported housing providers themselves, co-operation between developers, investors and publicly funded providers has become common.

The Czech marketing material found by the BBC said Nurture provides housing for people with mental health issues who receive the "aftercare program pursuant to Section 117 of the Mental Health Act", meaning they have been sectioned and discharged from hospital with a detailed care plan.

But Phil says he has never been sectioned under the Mental Health Act.

He does have severe depression and anxiety, and he is currently out of work. But he says he has never had any support or care, or met anyone working for Nurture during his time at the flat.

"Whoever marketed this property, the way they've worded it is total dishonesty," says Phil. "If they're looking to make as much profit as they can, then they clearly have no plans to fix the issues in the building."

Phil had no idea the flat he rents had been sold to overseas investors in May 2025 until the BBC contacted him. But there were clues: bills addressed to someone called Jan HÃ¡la had been coming through the letterbox for months.

Lee Jones told us that the properties his companies provide are "good quality accommodation" and he has no responsibility for the communal areas of Castleview House since he sold the freehold in 2021. He denied his relationship with Chris Smith amounted to a conflict of interest, but did not respond to questions about his role in marketing the properties.

Jan HÃ¡la, the Czech investor who now owns Phil's flat, and the BritskÃ© Reality estate agency did not respond to requests for comment.

We spoke to several other people living in flats run by Nurture Housing Association in Castleview House who said they were in supported accommodation. They reported receiving little or no help from Nurture but were afraid to speak out publicly for fear of eviction and becoming homeless.…

item.title: Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of lunch at work
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: light-hearted, but not particularly informative

Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of lunch at work

- Published

There are two types of office workers: those who eat lunch al-desko, and those who have to endure the smell of everyone else's.

Few things are more likely to test workplace relationships than the person sitting next to you proudly unveiling a container of reheated fish.

From tuna sandwiches and boiled eggs to crumbly and sticky treats that leave a mess on the keyboard, what is considered OK to eat in the office can be surprisingly divisive.

"We all know not to bring in a microwave fish pie, that is the law," says civil servant Sarah.

She admits she has, in fact, committed the offence herself in a previous workplace and jokes "that's the reason I left".

'Suss out the smelliness'

Casey, a content creator for an energy company, says he used to eat tuna at his desk but has since "reformed".

He says you have to "suss out the smelliness" and then decide if it's acceptable to eat at the desk.

But fish isn't the only food causing office friction and Casey says his regular snack of cinnamon pretzels has been causing "quite a bit of havoc".

"The sugar's going everywhere and it's getting in my laptop keys," he admits. No-one in the office has commented on it yet but he says he's hiding the crumbs by "shuffling them off the desk".

Boiled eggs also split opinion. Laura, who works in finance, says she's been teased by colleagues for eating them.

"In my defence, it was high protein, it was cost-effective and healthy â I swear by a good boiled egg."

She thinks that no food is off limits at the desk. "Coming from an Asian background where you'd eat fish for breakfast I am very open to it being eaten."

Ashlea Fisher, who runs her own recruitment company, has tackled the issue of smelly food in the office head on when she asked a member of staff to stop bringing in fish after "the smell was so bad that a pregnant colleague was feeling physically sick".

"I'm a big believer in being able to have an honest conversation with your team," she says, and suggests that other people in her position should approach a conversation lightly and be conscious of not embarrassing colleagues.

"Nobody should feel judged for what they eat, and we should respect different cultures and dietary requirements, but being mindful of the people around you is simply good workplace etiquette."

Do you take a lunch break?

While what we eat in the office at lunch can cause tension, there's also the question of whether we're even taking the time to enjoy our lunch in the first place.

In a world of back-to-back meetings and overflowing inboxes, it's easy to skip our break and shovel down a sandwich with one hand while replying to emails with the other.

A 2025 report by Just Eat found that the youngest workers, Gen Z, were the most likely to take a full break, with 56% doing so.

However, the next generation up, millennials were more likely than any other to eat lunch at their desk.

"While it can be convenient to eat at your desk, it's not best practice to remain glued to the screen all day," says Alan Price, an employment law and HR expert, and CEO of BrightHR.

"Taking a break isn't just an employment right, there are proven benefits for both physical and mental health."

Laura, whose working day can occasionally finish at 2am, says stepping away from her desk is a non-negotiable and she makes a point of taking an hour for lunch, describing it as "essential for maintaining my sanity".

"I take my lunch break as much as possible, for the sake of my eyes and mental wellbeing," she says.

But others are less precious about it. Content creator Manny says he has lunch at his desk "most of the time".

His work is task-based and his company operates a policy of "do the work when you want to do it".

"Usually you just take 20 minutes to eat something, but on another day you might take an hour. You just kind of feel it out," he says.

item.title: Judge extends deadline for Trump’s deposition in $10bn BBC lawsuit
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: legal news, but not directly related to business

Donald Trump has been granted a temporary delay before he must give a witness statement in his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC.

In late October, Enjoliqué Lett, a federal magistrate judge, gave Trump a firm 11 December deadline to sit for a deposition by lawyers representing the BBC in his lawsuit against the British broadcaster. If he failed to do so by that date, he could be subject to penalties up to dismissal of the case, the judge warned.

But on Tuesday, the president got something of a reprieve when Jeffrey Kuntz, a federal district court judge, approved a joint motion by the parties and extended the deadline for Trump’s deposition until 22 January. The judge also pushed back the deadline for discovery in the case from 18 December to 29 January.

Trump had originally agreed to sit for a deposition on 16 October, but his team backed out, citing “matters of national importance”. That led the BBC to file a motion to compel Trump to sit for a deposition in a timely fashion.

According to the joint motion filed on Monday, the BBC has agreed to the Trump team’s proposal for the president to sit for a deposition between 11 January and 22 January after his representatives said he was unavailable to do so this year “due to his schedule and the nature of his profession”. As that timeline nears, the parties will meet to select a date and identify a secure location for the deposition.

“It is Trump’s case, so he should expect to be deposed,” Kuntz wrote in his order. “It appears he acknowledges that reality.”

The judge ordered the parties to schedule Trump’s deposition by Friday at noon. Kuntz scheduled a trial date for the case for 3 May 2027 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

So far, Trump’s lawyers have deposed seven defendant witnesses. As part of the agreement between Trump and the BBC, the president’s lawyers will not depose Samir Shah, the BBC chair, or a former BBC director-general – nor any current or former BBC employee – until the president sits for questioning.

While Trump’s seven-hour-long deposition will be videotaped, it will only be available to attorneys for the parties.

In addition to Trump, the BBC might also be able to depose his daughter, Ivanka Trump, his son, Donald Trump Jr, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner. “Defendant is currently conferring with President Trump and these non-parties regarding the subpoenas directed to them, given that these non-parties may be objecting to, or moving to quash, those subpoenas,” the parties wrote in their joint motion.

Last week, Kuntz, a Trump appointee, refused the BBC’s request to dismiss the case, though he threw out the president’s contention that the broadcaster violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech.

“BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a 70-minute-long speech into 12 seconds,” the judge wrote in his ruling. “But the court is not persuaded.”
